claims.feature: first person as natural storytelling voice
claims.claim: Hobb chooses first person because it is the voice people use when telling family what happened today.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
claims.quote: the natural voice for the story teller

claims.claim: First person lets the reader be privy to the viewpoint character's innermost thoughts and feelings.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
claims.quote: privy to the characters innermost thoughts and feelings

claims.feature: first-person epistemic limit and dramatic irony
claims.claim: The reader knows only what the protagonist knows, yet may see what is coming before he does.
claims.quote: see what is coming even if the main character doesn't

claims.claim: In Farseer the chapter-opening prologues exist to give the reader information the first-person narrator cannot.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
claims.quote: little prologues at the beginning of each chapter

claims.claim: First person forbids the cutaway; everything must be learned as Fitz learns it.
She switched to third-person multiple viewpoint in Liveship only because important events happened at once in different places.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)

claims.claim: A hurt, physical or emotional, becomes baggage that alters later action, and the reader drags the same baggage through the reading.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
claims.quote: drags that same baggage through the reading

claims.claim: Other heroes' ordeals feel lesser because the event is not dwelt on and leaves no lingering change; Hobb dwells and lets it change the character.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
claims.quote: the event is not dwelt on

claims.claim: She denies being crueller than Tolkien; first person makes the same trials feel more harrowing because they are lived from inside.
claims.source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
claims.quote: perceived as more harrowing or depressing

claims.claim: Hobb describes her own style in two words, leisurely and intimate.
The pacing at the start of any of her books is deliberately much slower than toward the end.
claims.quote: usually a lot slower than towards the end

claims.claim: An exciting scene lacks impact unless she has slowed down to build the ramps up to it.
claims.quote: construct the ramps up to that exciting scene

claims.claim: She spends words on details and incidents that do not move the plot because they are what make the character.
claims.quote: not directly move the plot forward but are very important

claims.feature: show what is held before it is lost (consequence device)
claims.claim: A loss registers only if the text has first shown how much the lost thing mattered; otherwise the event is a throwaway moment.
claims.quote: this event is just a throwaway moment

claims.claim: Excitement and quick pace are sometimes sacrificed for character, knowingly.
claims.quote: have to be sacrificed for character

verdicts.trueWording: the natural voice for the story teller
verdicts.note: Aidan Moher raw page reached (HTTP 200). Quote exact. Both limbs on page: 'To me, the first person voice is the natural voice for the story teller. We use it often when we are telling family and friends what happened to day' (page's own typo for 'today').

verdicts.trueWording: privy to the characters innermost thoughts and feelings
verdicts.note: Quote exact and complete on the raw page: 'With first person, the reader gets to know the viewpoint character intimately because the reader is privy to the characters innermost thoughts and feelings.'

verdicts.trueWording: see what is coming even if the main character doesn't
verdicts.note: SFFWorld raw page reached (HTTP 200). Both limbs on page: 'The reader can only know exactly as much as the protagonist knows' and 'the reader will perhaps be able to see what is coming even if the main character doesn't.' Claim's 'may' preserves the page's 'perhaps' hedge.

verdicts.trueWording: little prologues at the beginning of each chapter
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Purpose limb supported in the same paragraph: 'the writer is limited to telling the reader what that character knows at that moment... In Farseer, I coped with that by having little prologues at the beginning of each chapter that gave the reader additional information.'

OF Blog raw page reached (HTTP 200); page header confirms 'Monday, April 28, 2003 / Robin Hobb Interview', matching the 2003 attribution. Q14: 'It was horribly inconvenient at times, because I could never say, "Meanwhile, back at the castle, thus and so was happening." I could only tell the reader what Fitz knew at that moment.' Both limbs supported.

Quote exact; page: 'In the Liveship books, I had a storyline where important events were occurring simultaneously in different places. Rather than limit the story to one person's experience... I decided to use third person and write from several points-of-view.' Simultaneity is the only reason the page gives for the switch, so the claim's 'only' stands; note the page also cites a second benefit (multiple perspectives on one event) as a consequence, not a cause.

verdicts.trueWording: drags that same baggage through the reading
verdicts.note: Quote exact; full support: 'When my characters get hurt, physically or emotionally, they acquire baggage and later on it may affect what they do. As the reader experiences the story, he drags that same baggage through the reading.' Claim's 'alters' is slightly firmer than the page's 'may affect'.

verdicts.trueWording: they seem lesser because the event is not dwelt on
verdicts.note: Quote exact and the first half is fully supported: 'many fantasy tales where the heroes or heroines endure some truly awful experiences, but they seem lesser because the event is not dwelt on, and in some cases, it doesn't seem to have lingering effects or change the character in any way.' Two gaps: (a) the page hedges 'in some cases' where the claim asserts flatly that such events leave no lingering change; (b) the page nowhere says Hobb dwells on the event - the nearest wording is 'the character experiences them deeply and thus the reader feels those events more strongly.' 'Lets it change the character' is supported by the adjacent baggage paragraph; the dwelling limb is inference.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Hobb herself dwells on the event - the page says only that her characters experience events deeply

verdicts.trueWording: perceived as more harrowing or depressing
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Denial limb: 'I don't think my characters endure anything that is more harrowing than, for example, the members of the Fellowship in the Lord of the Rings' and 'I don't think that I do exceptionally cruel things to my characters.' Lived-from-inside limb: the Boromir example, 'we would perceive his torment and his torn loyalties a lot more sharply than we do when we only see his actions.' Page names the Fellowship/LOTR rather than Tolkien by name.

Fantasy Book Critic raw page reached (HTTP 200); header confirms 'Monday, January 7, 2008 / Interview with Robin Hobb'. Page: 'I would describe my writing style as both leisurely and intimate.' Answering a direct question about her own style, so 'her own style, in two words' is exact.

verdicts.trueWording: usually a lot slower than towards the end
verdicts.note: Quote exact: 'The pacing at the beginning of any of my books is usually a lot slower than towards the end of the book, simply because so many words are given over to character construction.' The 'simply because...' clause carries the claim's 'deliberately'. The claim drops the page's 'usually' hedge, though the quote itself retains it.

verdicts.trueWording: construct the ramps up to that exciting scene
verdicts.note: Quote exact and every limb present: 'when I didn't slow down and construct the ramps up to that exciting scene, when I propelled the reader directly into it, it lacked the impact and significance I wanted it to have.'

verdicts.trueWording: may not directly move the plot forward but are very important
verdicts.note: Quote is an exact contiguous substring (page reads 'may not directly'). Purpose limb supported: '...very important to letting the reader know who the character is and thus why he makes the choices he does', introduced as 'the key to strong characterization is taking the time to develop the character. For me, that means putting in details and incidents that...'

verdicts.trueWording: this event is just a throwaway moment
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Full conditional on page via the Joe/Ed example: 'If I don't take the time to show you how important Ed is to Joe, and what interesting people they are, then this event is just a throwaway moment in the book.' The page's instance is a death; the claim generalises to 'the lost thing', which the surrounding argument supports.

verdicts.trueWording: Sometimes excitement and a quick pace have to be sacrificed
verdicts.note: Quote as supplied is NOT word for word: the page reads 'Sometimes excitement and a quick pace have to be sacrificed for the sake of creating a character that people can really know and identify with' - 'for character' is the sweep's compression of 'for the sake of creating a character'. Substance of every limb (sometimes, sacrificed, for character, as a knowing choice) is fully on the page, so VERIFIED_SUBSTANCE rather than VERIFIED_VERBATIM.
